source_document.body:
AI and digital fluency rank among the most needed procurement skills for 2030, but few leaders believe their teams are prepared for future demands, according to new research from Procurious . The report found that 82% identify AI and digital fluency as a priority, while only 28% say their teams are ready for what lies ahead.
What’s Related
The findings also show that training is struggling to keep pace. More than half of procurement teams have no structured, future-focused training plan, and 66% of respondents say their training budget is insufficient.
The report found that more than 90% of respondents say skills shortages already affect their ability to meet business objectives. Those concerns extend beyond learning how to use new technology to the commercial decisions procurement teams make.
“Closing the gap requires more than static curricula and occasional training,” said Tania Seary, founder of Procurious.
RELATED STORIES: Procurement Has Big AI Plans. Its Data Isn’t Ready | AI Is Reshaping Procurement Jobs, But Few Leaders Have Redesigned Them
Skills beyond AI
After AI and digital fluency, respondents identified working with and influencing people across the business (42%) and commercial judgement (39%) as priority skills for 2030. Those findings point to the importance of skills that extend beyond using technology.
“Procurement is a profession built on relationships, judgement and influence,” said Jade Cusworth, global learning and development director at Procurious+. “People develop those by pulling in outside expertise, working through real problems and comparing notes with peers who are facing the same ones.”
Respondents also pointed to consequences if skills shortages remain unaddressed over the next 12 to 24 months:
Compliance : 30% say regulatory compliance and efforts to reduce audit risk would suffer.
Revenue: 22% point to effects on outcomes such as time to market and supplier innovation .
Supply disruptions : 21% say disruptions would become harder to manage.
The concerns were more pronounced at larger businesses. Among respondents at companies with more than $5 billion in revenue, 45% say skills shortages create noticeable or significant challenges, compared with 36% overall.
No budget, no time
Nearly 60% of respondents lack a formal framework defining the procurement skills their teams need. More than half lack either the budget or the time and resources to develop and maintain training programs.
Even when training is available, people struggle to find time to participate. Workload prevents 52% of respondents from actively taking part in development opportunities.
Spending is uneven, too: 9% report investing nothing per employee, and 40% have no defined per-employee training budget. When asked what spending should be, 36% favor $2,000 or more, while another 21% favor $1,500 to $2,000.
Procurious founder Tania Seary said businesses need to commit resources to developing procurement teams as their responsibilities grow. “Procurement can't build that capability on its own. The business has to put time and money behind it.”
